Part E · Chapter 2

Encoders and CLIP

An image encoder and a text encoder trained together, so that a photo can be compared with captions

An encoder turns a photo or a text into a vector. CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder together on captioned photos, so that a photo has a higher cosine with its own caption than with other captions. A caption can name a new class without new training. The tests use CLIP ViT-B/32 on 14 photos and a masked autoencoder on two. Photos are credited under the figures.

You will need: vision transformers (E1), cosine similarity (D2, 0.5), softmax and temperature (0.7), cross-entropy (D3) and murky water (C3).

What an encoder does

Guess first. A photo of a hammerhead and the words "a scalloped hammerhead swimming in open blue water" are different kinds of data. How could a computer test whether they match?

An encoder is a neural network that turns an input into one vector, a list of 512 numbers here, also called an embedding. The cosine similarity (cosine for short) of two vectors \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) is their dot product divided by the product of their lengths. The dot product sums the products of their numbers in pairs. CLIP has an image encoder for photos and a text encoder for text. Training adjusts them together so that the vector of a photo has a higher cosine with the vector of its own caption than with those of other captions.

  1. The strips show the first 40 of the 512 numbers of the photo vector and the text vector. The boxes under them give their cosine for the hammerhead photo in blue water and “a photo of a scalloped hammerhead shark”: 0.337.
  2. The list ranks the nine species prompts, texts of the form “a photo of a ...”, by cosine with the photo: hammerhead first at 0.337, milk shark second at 0.331. Click the dolphin thumbnail: “a photo of a dolphin” has the highest cosine, 0.044 above the next.

Photo vector, the first 40 of 512 numbers (teal positive, coral negative)

Text vector, the first 40 of 512 numbers

Cosine of this photo with the nine species prompts "a photo of a ..." (the chosen text is outlined if it is one of them)

Credits of the 14 photos

    For the hammerhead photo the nine species prompts have cosines from 0.205 to 0.337, and the top two differ by only 0.006.

    How it works

    Take the hammerhead photo and the text “a photo of a scalloped hammerhead shark”. The image encoder gives the photo a vector \(\mathbf{u}\) and the text encoder gives the text a vector \(\mathbf{v}\), both of 512 numbers. The length of \(\mathbf{u}\) is the square root of the sum of its squared numbers. Both vectors are scaled to length 1, so their cosine equals their dot product. This is the sum of the 512 products \(u_j v_j\), where \(u_j\) is the \(j\)-th number of \(\mathbf{u}\). For this pair the sum is 0.337.

    cos(\(\mathbf{u}\), \(\mathbf{v}\))cosine: 0.337=\(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\)the dot product: 0.337÷ (\(\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\)length of \(\mathbf{u}\): 1.00×\(\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert\)length of \(\mathbf{v}\): 1.00)

    A cosine is 1 when two vectors point the same way, so 0.337 is small, yet it is the highest of the nine prompts for this photo. So what matters is the comparison with other texts, and a cosine is not a probability. On average over the 14 photos, a photo and its own caption have a cosine of 0.32, and a photo and the captions of other photos 0.22.

    Common belief. CLIP reads the caption, looks at the photo, and then decides whether they match.

    Why it fails. Neither encoder receives the input of the other, so the only comparison is one dot product afterwards.

    Better account. CLIP is two separate encoders and one cheap comparison.

    Quick quiz

    Why can one photo vector be compared with many captions without running the image encoder again?

    The image encoder never receives the caption, so the vector of the photo does not depend on it. A new caption needs one text encoding and one dot product.

    The cosine of a photo with its own caption is about 0.32. Does that show a weak match?

    Not by itself. A cosine ranks the texts for one photo, and what counts is the difference from the other captions: 0.32 against 0.22 on average for these 14 photos.

    Go deeper how the encoders are built, symbols, Python about 3 min

    How the two encoders are built

    The photo goes through the image encoder, the first of the two towers of CLIP. In this model it is a ViT-B/32 (E1). The photo is cut into 49 patches of 32 by 32 pixels and a class token is added. Twelve blocks follow, and a linear layer turns the class vector into 512 numbers. The text goes through the text encoder, the second tower, a transformer with 12 layers, width 512 and 8 heads. The text is split into tokens (D1; the CLIP paper gives a vocabulary of 49,152), and a start and an end token are added. The encoder uses a causal mask (D4), and its vector for the text is the vector at the end token. The image tower and the text tower have 87.8 million and 63.4 million numbers (counted from the released model). A photo can be encoded once and compared with any number of texts later, which makes zero-shot classification and photo search fast.

    Symbols

    \[ \cos(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert} = \sum_{j=1}^{512} u_j v_j \quad\text{when}\quad \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert = \lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert = 1 \]

    • \(\mathbf{u}\) is the vector of the photo and \(\mathbf{v}\) the vector of the text, both with 512 numbers. \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) is the length of a vector (0.5).
    • With unit length vectors the lengths are 1 and the cosine is the sum of 512 products. A typical number in a unit vector of 512 numbers has size about \(1/\sqrt{512} = 0.044\), which is why the strips above are pale.

    A second look at the average cosines

    The same network gives four average cosines on the 14 photos of this chapter. A photo with another photo gives 0.71. A caption with another caption gives 0.51. A photo with its own caption gives 0.32, and a photo with the captions of the other photos gives 0.22. A matching pair is only 0.10 above the mismatched pairs and far below the 0.71 of photo to photo. Photos and texts have vectors in one space but do not mix evenly, and the shared space section shows this. Where it works: the names of the nine species can be compared with the photos directly. An ImageNet classifier has a fixed list of 1,000 outputs and cannot name anything outside it. Where it breaks: a cosine shows only which of two texts is more like the photo, and it has no probability scale.

    Common mistakes

    Debug tip. Compare vectors only when they come from the same model and have the same length. A longer vector gives a larger dot product even when its content is no closer, so scale to length 1 first. The cosine between vectors from two different CLIP models, or from CLIP and a sentence encoder like the one in D2, has no meaning, because the models do not share a space.

    In Python

    import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4127)
u = rng.normal(size=512)                         # made-up photo vector
v = 0.3 * u + rng.normal(size=512)               # made-up text vector that shares some of its signal
u = u / np.linalg.norm(u); v = v / np.linalg.norm(v)    # scale both to length 1
print(round(float(np.linalg.norm(u)), 1), round(float(u @ v), 3))
print(round(float(np.sqrt((u ** 2).mean())), 3))       # the typical size of one of the 512 numbers
    1.0 0.26
0.044

    These two vectors are made up. Their cosine is the dot product once both have length 1, and the typical number in a unit vector of 512 numbers is 0.044, as above.

    Three ways to train an encoder

    Guess first. To train an image encoder you need a task with a known target. Name two such tasks, and say what they would cost to prepare.

    An encoder is trained on a task with a known target, the correct output, and three kinds of task are common. In the first, people attach a label to photos, a name such as “hammerhead”, and the network is trained to give the true label a high probability. In masked prediction, part of a photo is hidden and the network is trained to rebuild it. The hidden part is then the target, so no person writes a label. In CLIP, contrastive learning uses photos paired with captions, and the network is trained to tell which caption belongs to which photo.

    1. On the “Masked prediction” tab the photo is cut into small squares, the patches. The left picture shows the patches the encoder gets (hidden ones grey), and the right picture shows the network’s guess for them. At 75% hidden the error for the Costa Rica hammerhead is 3.7.
    2. Drag “Share of patches hidden” to 90%: the guess becomes a blur. Then drag it back to 75% and choose the bamboo shark: its error is 17.1.
    3. On the “Labels” tab, the probability 0.88 for the true label gives a loss of 0.13, the number that training lowers.

    The photo has a label chosen from a list of 1,000 names. The network gives 1,000 scores, softmax turns them into probabilities, and the loss is the cross-entropy of next-token prediction: the negative log of the probability given to the true label.

    What the encoder sees (grey patches are hidden)

    The network's guess for the whole photo

    No list of labels. The data is pairs: a photo and the caption written for it. The network must tell which caption belongs to which photo in a batch (next section).

    A photo should be nearest to its own caption and far from the others. These three pairs are from this chapter's photos.

    At 75% hidden the error, the average difference in pixel brightness (0 to 255) between guess and photo, is 3.7 for the Costa Rica hammerhead and 17.1 for the bamboo shark.

    How it works

    Take the label method on a hammerhead photo. The network gives one score per name on a list of 1,000 names, and the softmax turns them into probabilities that add to 1. If the true label gets the probability p = 0.88, the loss is −ln p = 0.13, where ln is the natural logarithm (Part 0). The loss falls as p rises and is 0 only when p = 1, since ln 1 = 0.

    \(-\ln p_y\)labels: \(p_y\) is the probability of the true label \(y\)|mean \((\hat x - x)^2\)masked: \(x\) the true pixels of a hidden patch, \(\hat x\) the guess, averaged over the hidden patches; the figure reports the mean absolute difference as the error

    Common belief. A network that rebuilds a photo well has learned what is in it.

    Why it fails. Much of the Costa Rica hammerhead photo is flat blue water, which is probably easy to rebuild from neighbouring patches. So its low error of 3.7 may say little about the shark, and the figure does not give the error for the shark alone. Neither error shows whether the encoder would separate a hammerhead from a milk shark.

    Better account. Rebuilding is a training task, so whether the vectors are useful is tested afterwards on a task that matters. An example is sorting photos into species when only a few photos have labels.

    Quick quiz

    Which of the three methods needs a list of names fixed in advance, and where does masked prediction get its targets?

    The label method needs the list (1,000 names in the example). Masked prediction takes its targets from the photo itself, the pixels of the hidden patches, so no person writes a label. Contrastive learning needs pairs but no list, since the caption is free text.

    The network gives the true label the probability 0.5. What is the loss, and for which probability is it 0?

    The loss is −ln 0.5 = ln 2 = 0.69. It is 0 when the probability is 1, since ln 1 = 0.

    Go deeper the three methods, symbols, a debug tip about 3 min

    Labels

    This is the supervised learning of A1. The torchvision ViT-B/16 of E1 was trained on ImageNet-1k, whose labels cover 1,000 names and 1.28 million training photos (the CLIP paper gives the second number). A network trained on a fixed list of labels can only name things on the list. This one has three shark classes and no spadenose shark class, and in E1 it called the spadenose crop an eel. A network that guessed among the 1,000 names would give p = 1/1,000 and a loss of ln 1,000 = 6.91.

    Masked prediction

    BERT (D5) picks 15% of the tokens of a text, replaces most of them by a [MASK] symbol and predicts the originals (Devlin and others, 2019). The masked autoencoder (MAE, He and others, 2022) does the same for photos. It hides 75% of the patches of a photo and runs the encoder on the visible patches only. A small decoder gets the encoder's output and one placeholder per hidden patch, and it rebuilds the pixels. The loss is the mean squared error on the hidden patches only. The slider shows reconstructions made by a trained network. At 25% hidden the guess is close. At 90% hidden the guess is a blur: the shark is a smudge in about the right place, and the bands on the bamboo shark are gone. No person wrote a label, so a collection of photos is enough. Training with targets taken from the data itself is called self-supervised. The ViT paper tried a simpler version of the idea in a first test, predicting the mean colour of hidden patches. ViT-B/16 reached 79.9% on ImageNet, 2 points above training from scratch and 4 points below supervised pre-training (Dosovitskiy and others, 2021).

    Contrastive pairs

    CLIP uses 400 million image and text pairs collected from the internet (Radford and others, 2021). The caption takes the place of the label, and it was written by the people who posted or described the photo, so it can name anything. Cost: the pairs are noisy, since a caption may be wrong or say little, and a model trained on them can reflect what people post and how they describe it. The model card of the released model lists deployed use as out of scope and warns that its results change with the class list. The rest of the chapter treats it as a model to test.

    How the figure measures the error

    The error in the figure is the mean absolute difference between the guess and the photo over the hidden pixels, on a scale of 0 to 255, while the loss squares the differences. Reconstructions are from facebook/vit-mae-base, with the same random mask for both photos. The photos are two crops of 224 by 224 pixels, cut into 196 patches of 16 by 16 pixels. The figure opens on masked prediction because that tab has pictures.

    Symbols

    \[ \ell_{\text{label}} = -\ln p_y,\qquad L_{\text{mask}} = \frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{i\in H}\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i-\mathbf{x}_i\rVert^2 \]

    • \(p_y\) is the probability that softmax gives to the true label \(y\) (0.7).
    • \(H\) is the set of hidden patches, \(\mathbf{x}_i\) the true pixels of patch \(i\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i\) the network's guess for them.

    Common mistakes

    Debug tip. If a masked-prediction run reaches a very low loss at the start, check that the loss counts the hidden patches only. Averaged over all patches it also counts the visible ones, which the network can copy.

    More questions

    Why does MAE hide as much as 75% of the patches?

    Neighbouring patches are alike, so hiding few of them makes the task a matter of copying. With most of the photo hidden the network must use what it has learned about objects. He and others (2022) report that this ratio works well, and it also makes the encoder cheaper, since it reads only a quarter of the patches.

    CLIP's similarity matrix

    Guess first. You have a batch of N photos with their N captions. You write the cosines of all photos with all captions in a table with a row per photo and a column per caption. Which entries should be high, and what should be true of a row?

    A training step of CLIP uses a batch, N photos with their own captions. The similarity matrix is the N × N table of the cosines of all photos (rows) with all captions (columns), so its diagonal contains the true pairs. The contrastive loss, a number that training lowers, is low when in all rows and all columns the diagonal entry is clearly the largest. Training adjusts both encoders to lower it.

    1. Press “Pick 6 different animals”. The coral outlines mark the diagonal. The cosine on it is the highest in its row and column, and the loss is only 0.006.
    2. Press “Pick all 14”: the loss is 0.762. Click row p8, the hammerhead from Costa Rica, and the boxes under the matrix work out its loss, about 1.75.
    3. Then choose the chip “T = 1” (T is the temperature, explained in the next section). The loss rises to 2.543, near ln 14 = 2.639, the loss when all 14 captions get the same probability.

    Choose the batch: click photos to add or remove them (at least two). A photo brings its own caption.

      The loss of this batch

      The working for the selected row (click a row)

      Captions were written for this chapter from the Wikimedia descriptions of the photos.

      Credits of the 14 photos

        The loss is 0.006 for six different animals and 0.762 for all 14 photos, where the own caption is the top choice for only 9 of 14 photos.

        How it works

        Take photo p8, the Costa Rica hammerhead, in the batch of 14. Its own caption has the cosine 0.325, and the caption of the other hammerhead photo 0.340. Cosines are divided by the temperature T, 0.01 in the model used here, and the results, 32.5 and 34.0, are called logits. A softmax gives a logit z the probability ez divided by the sum of ez over the 14 logits of the row. For the own caption, p = e32.5 / (e32.5 + e34.0 + the other 12 terms) = 0.174. The loss of the row is −ln p = 1.75.

        Row p8:0.325cosine on the diagonal÷0.01temperature \(T\)=32.5logit→ softmax over the row →0.174\(p\) of its own caption→1.75loss of the row, \(-\ln p\)

        The row loss measures how well a photo finds its own caption among the captions, and the column loss does the same for a caption among the photos. The loss of the batch is the mean of the average row loss, 0.620, and the average column loss, 0.905, so it is 0.762.

        Common belief. The loss pushes all photos and all captions to the same vector.

        Why it fails. If all vectors were equal, all cosines would be equal, so all rows would give probability 1/N. The loss would then be ln N, the chance level of a model with no information.

        Better account. The loss is low when the true pair has a higher cosine than the other pairs in the batch. No pair needs a cosine of 1.

        Quick quiz

        What is the loss of a batch of 8 when all entries of the matrix are equal?

        All rows and columns give probability 1/8 to the diagonal entry, so the loss is ln 8 = 2.08.

        Why are the rows and the columns both used?

        The rows measure how well a photo finds its caption among the captions, and the columns how well a caption finds its photo among the photos. The two questions differ, so the loss uses both.

        Go deeper terms, a worked row, symbols, Python about 4 min

        Terms

        positive pair, negative pair
        a photo with its own caption (the diagonal), and with any other caption (the rest)

        Reading the figure

        For the six different animals the diagonal beats the best rival in its row by 0.03 to 0.18. The 14 photos include pairs that a caption describes equally well: two hammerheads, two milk sharks, two Ganges drawings. With all 14 pairs, the own caption is the top choice for 9 of the 14 photos, and the own photo is the top choice for 10 of 14 captions. The five rows whose own caption is not on top have losses from 0.97 to 2.10, and the nine rows where it is on top have 0.67 or less. Adding the second hammerhead and the second milk shark photo to the six animals raises the loss from 0.006 to 0.691. A likely reason is that two captions then fit one photo: the caption of the other hammerhead photo (0.340) outscores the own caption of the second one (0.325).

        A worked row, step by step

        With rounded cosines, row p8 of the batch of 14 has the diagonal cosine 0.325 and the best rival 0.340. At T = 0.01 the logits are 32.5 and 34.0, and the difference is 1.5. The other 12 captions get 0.6% of the probability between them, so the true caption gets about 1 / (1 + e1.5) = 0.18, and the loss of that row is about −ln 0.18 = 1.7. The figure uses the unrounded cosines and shows 0.174 and 1.75.

        Symbols

        \[ L = -\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\ln\frac{e^{s_{ii}/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}e^{s_{ij}/T}} + \ln\frac{e^{s_{ii}/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}e^{s_{ji}/T}}\right],\qquad s_{ij} = \cos(\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{v}_j) \]

        • \(\mathbf{u}_i\) is the vector of photo \(i\) and \(\mathbf{v}_j\) the vector of caption \(j\). \(s_{ij}\) is their cosine, the entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) of the matrix.
        • The first term is the softmax over row \(i\): which caption belongs to photo \(i\). The second is the softmax over column \(i\): which photo belongs to caption \(i\).
        • \(T\) is the temperature (D3). The CLIP paper writes \(\tau\). Training adjusts it, and it is clipped so that dividing by it never multiplies by more than 100, which means \(T \ge 0.01\). The released model has the value 100 for the multiplier, so \(T = 0.01\).
        • The "chance level" in the boxes is \(\ln N\), the loss when all entries of a row are equal. The form is the InfoNCE loss of van den Oord and others (2018), used with a batch of 32,768 pairs by Radford and others (2021).

        Why the batch is large

        A photo is compared with N − 1 wrong captions in its row. All of them are negative examples that cost no extra encoding, since they are already in the batch. A larger batch makes the task harder, which usually helps the vectors that the encoders learn. With 32,768 pairs the matrix has 1,073,741,824 entries, and the loss still needs only the two encoders run 32,768 times. Where it misleads: a caption that fits two photos is a negative for one of them, and the loss punishes the network for a reasonable choice.

        Common mistakes

        Debug tip. A contrastive loss that stays at \(\ln N\) shows that the network has not learned to tell the pairs apart. Look for a batch where captions are shuffled relative to photos, or for vectors that are not scaled to length 1. A loss near zero early on can mean that captions contain identifiers of the photos, or that the test photos are also in the training set.

        In Python

        import numpy as np
# cosine of 4 photos (rows) and their own captions (columns), from CLIP ViT-B/32:
# two hammerheads, then two milk sharks
S = np.array([[0.320, 0.318, 0.241, 0.238],
              [0.340, 0.325, 0.211, 0.212],
              [0.242, 0.254, 0.324, 0.329],
              [0.165, 0.167, 0.265, 0.280]])
def cross_entropy_diag(L):
    L = L - L.max(1, keepdims=True)                  # stable softmax over each row
    log_p = L - np.log(np.exp(L).sum(1, keepdims=True))
    return -np.diag(log_p).mean()                    # the true pair is on the diagonal
def clip_loss(S, T):
    L = S / T
    return (cross_entropy_diag(L) + cross_entropy_diag(L.T)) / 2
for T in (1, 0.1, 0.01):
    print(T, round(clip_loss(S, T), 4))
print(S.argmax(1))     # the caption each photo likes best
        1 1.3399
0.1 1.0375
0.01 1.3646
[0 0 3 3]

        Chance for 4 pairs is ln 4 = 1.386, and T = 1 is close to it (1.34), since all cosines then look alike. Photos 2 and 3 pick the wrong caption, so at T = 0.01 the loss (1.36) is higher than at T = 0.1 (1.04). A low temperature stretches the gaps in the logits, so a wrong top choice costs more.

        Temperature

        Guess first. The cosines of the hammerhead photo in blue water with the nine species prompts lie between 0.205 and 0.337. If a softmax turns them directly into probabilities, what will the nine probabilities look like? What could you divide the cosines by to make the top name clear?

        A softmax turns scores into probabilities that add to 1, and larger scores get larger probabilities. The nine cosines are close together, so a softmax of them directly gives nearly equal probabilities. CLIP first divides the cosines by the temperature T, and a cosine divided by T is a logit. Dividing by T keeps the order of the cosines, so the top caption stays on top. A small T multiplies the differences by 1/T, so at T = 0.01 a difference of 0.01 in cosine becomes a difference of 1 in logits.

        1. Drag the slider to T = 1: the nine bars lie between 10% and 12%.
        2. Press “Set T = 0.01 (the learned value)”, the value that training gave T: the hammerhead caption gets 46% and the milk shark caption 26%.
        3. Choose “Ganges, 1839 drawing”, which shows a Ganges shark: the top bar is the spadenose shark, a wrong caption, at 64%. Move T to 0.001 and its probability rises to 100%.

        At T = 1 the nine probabilities lie between 10% and 12%, and at T = 0.01 the hammerhead caption gets 46%, with the milk shark caption next at 26%.

        How it works

        Take the two best cosines for the hammerhead photo, 0.337 and 0.331. The softmax gives caption k the probability \(p_k = e^{s_k/T} / \sum_j e^{s_j/T}\), where \(s_k\) is the cosine of the photo with caption \(k\) and \(j\) runs over the nine captions. So the odds of two captions, the ratio of their probabilities, equal \(e\) raised to the difference in logits. At T = 1 the odds are e0.006 = 1.006, nearly even. With T = 0.01 the difference in logits is 0.6 and the odds are e0.6 = 1.8. With T = 0.001 it is 6 and the odds are e6 = 403. The figure keeps the unrounded cosines, so its boxes show 0.58 and 1.79 at T = 0.01 and 5.8 and 330 at T = 0.001.

        Top two:0.337cosine of the top caption−0.331cosine of the second=0.006difference in cosine÷0.01temperature \(T\)=0.6difference in logits→ odds\(e^{0.6} = 1.8\)top : second

        Training adjusts T along with the encoders, but the CLIP authors do not let it go below 0.01, the value of the model used here. The 46% at T = 0.01 comes from differences in cosine. This chapter has not checked whether top captions with a probability of 46% are right in 46% of cases.

        Common belief. A temperature is a setting for choosing the next word of a language model, and unrelated to how a model is trained.

        Why it fails. In CLIP the temperature is inside the loss, where it sets how sharply a difference of 0.01 in cosine is rewarded or punished.

        Better account. The same number has two roles: it sets the training signal, and later it turns cosines into probabilities.

        Quick quiz

        The top two cosines differ by 0.02. At T = 0.01, how many times likelier is the top one?

        The gap in logits is 0.02 / 0.01 = 2, and the odds are e2 = 7.4.

        Does lowering T change which caption is on top?

        No. Division by a positive number keeps the order. It changes how much of the probability the top caption takes.

        Go deeper effective number, how CLIP sets T, Python about 2 min

        Terms

        effective number of choices
        e raised to the entropy; the number of equal choices that would be as uncertain (D3)

        Reading the figure

        The slider moves T from 1 down to 0.001. The cosines do not change: they are the same nine numbers (the hammerhead photo against “a photo of a ...” and a species name). Only the division changes. The figure uses the unrounded cosines, so its boxes show 5.8 and 330 at T = 0.001. Odds grow fast with the gap, so a small rounding changes them a lot. The teal bar is the caption that names the species of the photo, and the outlined row is the top call. The readout under the bars gives the effective number of captions in play, eH.

        How CLIP sets T

        The temperature is not set by hand: training adjusts it. It starts at 0.07 and is stopped from going below 0.01, because the paper found that a larger multiplier made training unstable (Radford and others, 2021). The released model has reached the limit, 0.01. Two practical notes. A model that is well trained for a ranking can give poor probabilities, so a probability of 46% at T = 0.01 should be checked as a frequency before anyone relies on it (A4, calibrated). Using the same temperature in the loss and in zero-shot classification keeps the two consistent, because the model was trained to get its matches right when the logits were stretched by 100.

        Symbols

        \[ p_k = \frac{e^{s_k/T}}{\sum_{j} e^{s_j/T}},\qquad H = -\sum_k p_k \ln p_k,\qquad N_{\text{eff}} = e^{H} \]

        • \(s_k\) is the cosine of the photo with caption \(k\) and \(p_k\) the probability of caption \(k\). \(H\) is the entropy of the nine probabilities (D3), and \(N_{\text{eff}}\) the effective number of choices.
        • If \(T\) is large, all the \(s_k/T\) are near 0 and \(p_k \approx 1/9\). If \(T\) is small, the largest cosine takes all the probability.

        In Python

        import numpy as np
names = ["spadenose", "milk", "bamboo", "hammerhead", "Ganges", "eagle ray", "dolphin", "clownfish", "sea turtle"]
cos = np.array([0.322, 0.331, 0.238, 0.337, 0.328, 0.289, 0.276, 0.205, 0.245])   # hammerhead photo against "a photo of a ..."
def softmax(z):
    e = np.exp(z - z.max())
    return e / e.sum()
for T in (0.01, 1.0):
    p = softmax(cos / T)
    print(T, names[p.argmax()], np.round(p, 3))
        0.01 hammerhead [0.102 0.251 0.    0.457 0.186 0.004 0.001 0.    0.   ]
1.0 hammerhead [0.115 0.116 0.106 0.117 0.116 0.111 0.11  0.102 0.107]

        These cosines are rounded to three decimals, so the probabilities differ by a point or two from the figure, which uses the unrounded values.

        The shared space

        Guess first. Photos and captions are trained to match, so you may expect one mixed cloud, with a caption near its photo. Project the 512 numbers to 2 dimensions: do the points mix, or do photos and texts form two groups?

        Both encoders put their vectors in one space of 512 numbers, the shared space. To draw it we use PCA, a projection to 2 dimensions that keeps as much of the spread (variance) of the points as possible. Its first axis keeps the most. In this sample, the 14 photo vectors and the 32 text vectors form two separate clouds in the 512-number space. The distance between the clouds is the modality gap (a modality is a kind of data). The average photo vector and the average text vector are 0.93 apart, and two vectors of length 1 are at most 2 apart.

        1. On “As computed”, round markers with a photo inside are the 14 photos and diamonds are texts: the photos group at the left, the texts spread to the right.
        2. Press “Groups centred”, which removes the average of the photos and the average of the texts: the two clouds now overlap. A second PCA, made on the centred vectors, has a first axis that keeps 14% of the spread (35% in the first map).
        3. Click a photo or a text to list its five nearest texts or photos by cosine.
        Credits of the 14 photos

          As computed, photos and texts separate along the first axis, which keeps 35% of the spread; with the group averages removed, a second PCA keeps 14% on its first axis.

          How it works

          Take the 14 photos and their captions, with the average cosines in the boxes below. Vectors of the same kind are close: for all 14 photos the nearest other photo has a cosine of 0.73 to 0.92, the nearest text at most 0.36. Vectors of different kinds are farther apart, even a photo and its own caption.

          Mean cosines:0.71photo to photo|0.51caption to caption|0.32photo to its own caption|0.22photo to the other captions

          Because of the gap, a small cosine between a photo and a text does not mean “no match”. Judge it against the cosines of the same photo with other texts. The highest photo-to-text cosine here is 0.36, and for 9 of the 14 photos the own caption has the highest cosine of the 14 captions.

          Analogy. Picture a city map with photos of places and the names of places. A name should lie near its photo.

          Where it breaks. On the PCA map all the names are on one side and all the photos on the other. A name is usually nearer to its own photo than to other photos (10 of the 14 captions here). Even so, the cosine of a name with its own photo is low (0.32 on average). The map is a flat view of 512 dimensions, so nearness on it is only a rough guide.

          Quick quiz

          Do photos and captions form one mixed cloud in CLIP?

          No. They form two clouds with a gap between them. A photo is nearer to other photos than to any text, and a caption is usually, not always, nearest to its own photo among the photos.

          The cosine of a photo with its caption is 0.32. How do you judge it?

          By comparison with the cosines of the same photo with other captions. Photo-to-text cosines are all low in this model (at most 0.36 here), so 0.32 is not weak.

          Go deeper what the map shows, the gap, Python about 2 min

          What the map shows

          The map shows the 14 photos (round, with the photo inside), their 14 batch captions (coral diamonds), the nine species prompts (sand, labelled) and nine other texts (grey). The 512 numbers were projected to two axes by PCA, so the map keeps only part of the structure. As computed, the two axes keep 35% and 9% of the spread. Press "Zoom on the photos" to see them apart: the same map, rescaled, with the texts out of view. Then press "Groups centred": the average photo vector is subtracted from all photo vectors, the average text vector from all text vectors, and a second PCA is made on the centred vectors. Both clouds are then centred on nearly the same point, so they overlap by construction, and the first two axes keep 14% and 10% of the spread. Some photos then lie next to texts about the same subject, such as the Ganges drawings next to “a photo of a Ganges shark”, and others do not: the nearest text of the hammerhead photos on the map is a milk shark caption. The readout lists the cosines of the original vectors, and only the picture moves.

          Why there is a gap

          Liang and others (2022) name two causes. The encoders start with vectors in narrow cones, so the two kinds of vector begin apart. Contrastive training then keeps them apart, by a distance that depends on the temperature.

          Common mistakes

          Debug tip. When you project embeddings, say what the axes keep. The first two axes here keep 35% and 9% of the spread, so two points that look close on the map can be far apart in 512 numbers. Check with the cosines (the readout lists them).

          In Python

          import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4127)
common = rng.normal(size=512); common /= np.linalg.norm(common)
side = rng.normal(size=512); side /= np.linalg.norm(side)
photos = 0.7 * common + 0.45 * side + rng.normal(0, 0.02, size=(14, 512))    # made-up photo vectors in one cone
texts = 0.7 * common - 0.45 * side + rng.normal(0, 0.02, size=(14, 512))     # made-up text vectors in another
photos /= np.linalg.norm(photos, axis=1, keepdims=True)
texts /= np.linalg.norm(texts, axis=1, keepdims=True)
print(round(float(np.linalg.norm(photos.mean(0) - texts.mean(0))), 2))      # distance between the two averages
print(round(float((photos @ photos.T).mean()), 2), round(float((photos @ texts.T).mean()), 2))
pc, tc = photos - photos.mean(0), texts - texts.mean(0)                     # remove each group's average
print(round(float(np.linalg.norm(pc.mean(0) - tc.mean(0))), 2))
          0.96
0.79 0.33
0.0

          These vectors are made up, in two cones, with numbers chosen to look like the CLIP figures above. The two averages are 0.96 apart, close to the 0.93 of CLIP, photos resemble photos (0.79) more than they resemble texts (0.33), and removing the average of a group closes the gap. In the CLIP model the cosine between a photo and a text still ranks the matching caption first for 9 of the 14 photos.

          Zero-shot classification

          Guess first. CLIP was trained on photos with captions, with no fixed list of classes. You give it a photo and five species names. How would you get probabilities for the names, and what would it do with similar sharks?

          In zero-shot classification, the classes (the categories to choose from, here species) are named in text when the model is used. The model was not trained on them with labels. We write a candidate caption per class, usually a prompt template such as “a photo of a ...” filled with the class name. Then we encode the photo and the captions, divide the cosines by the temperature T = 0.01 and take a softmax over the captions. The list of captions sets the classes of the classifier, which returns the top caption, the one with the highest probability.

          1. Teal dots on the photos mark a right top caption, coral dots a wrong one. With all nine species captions and “a photo of a ...” the line below the bars says 9 of 14 right, and the ten shark photos have 5 teal dots.
          2. Press “Five sharks” and click through the photos: both spadenose photos are wrong, and both Ganges drawings are called spadenose.
          3. Press “All nine”, choose the hammerhead photo in blue water and untick “scalloped hammerhead shark”: the true class is not offered, and the top caption becomes milk shark at 47%.

          Photo (dots show whether the model is right on that photo with the captions below)

          Candidate captions (tick the ones to offer)

          Probability of the captions, T = 0.01

          Credits of the 14 photos

            With nine captions the top caption is a shark caption for all 10 shark photos and a non-shark caption for the other 4, but it names the right species for only 5 sharks.

            How it works

            Take the photo of spadenose sharks in a basket with the five shark captions. The cosines are 0.2929 (spadenose), 0.2893 (milk), 0.2571 (bamboo), 0.2695 (hammerhead) and 0.2990 (Ganges). At T = 0.01 the logits are 29.29, 28.93, 25.71, 26.95 and 29.90, and the softmax gives 0.27, 0.19, 0.01, 0.03 and 0.50. The top caption is the Ganges shark, so it is wrong, and the true class gets 0.27.

            Top caption:0.299cosine÷ 0.01 =29.9logit→ softmax over 5 captions →50%probability of the top caption

            The probabilities add to 1 over the captions offered, so the top caption is one of them even when the true class is missing. Offered only “dolphin”, “sea turtle” and “clownfish”, the hammerhead photo in blue water is called a dolphin with probability 0.96. The same photo gets a different top caption when the list changes, so the list is part of the classifier.

            Common belief. Zero-shot means the model knows the class without having seen it.

            Why it fails. The model was trained on many photos paired with words, so a class is zero-shot only for the labels of this task.

            Better account. Zero-shot means no training with the labels of this task. A name that is rare in captions may leave little to learn from, but this chapter did not count captions.

            Quick quiz

            What is the classifier in zero-shot CLIP?

            The two encoders, the list of captions and the softmax together. The list sets the classes: change the list and you change the classifier, with no training.

            A clownfish photo is offered only the captions “a photo of a milk shark” and “a photo of a hammerhead shark”. What does CLIP return?

            One of the two, with probabilities that add to 100%. The true class is not offered, so the top caption is wrong whatever the probabilities.

            Go deeper templates, the class list, symbols, Python about 3 min

            Reading the figure

            The method has no new training. The caption of a class is its name placed in a template. The paper reports that the frame "A photo of a {label}." often helps, and by 1.3% on ImageNet. For ImageNet it also averages the text vectors of 80 different templates, which adds 3.5% more (Radford and others, 2021). Try the three templates on the chips above. On these 14 photos the species count is 5 of 10 for “a photo of a ...”, 4 of 10 for the bare names and 3 of 10 with “in murky water” added, and in all three the top caption is a shark caption for all 10 shark photos. The counts differ by one or two photos, so do not read much into the order. With “Five sharks” the model mixes up the shark species: both spadenose photos are wrong (one gets milk shark, the other Ganges shark), and both drawings of the Ganges shark are called a spadenose. Press “Shark, fish or person”. Now 8 of the 10 shark photos are called “a photo of a shark”. So is the dolphin, and two shark photos, in a tank and on ice, are called fish. Coarse classes are easier than species, and still not safe.

            The class list is part of the model

            The Ganges shark is the rarest of the five species of the made-up catch table (A4 treats rare classes). The class list is part of the model: the same photo gets a different answer when the list changes, because softmax shares 100% among the candidates offered. If the true class is missing, the top caption is a wrong one, and it can have a high probability. The model card of the released model says the same: performance changes with the class list, so any use needs tests on the class list you will use.

            Symbols

            \[ \hat{y} = \arg\max_k\, \cos(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}_k),\qquad p(k\mid\text{photo}) = \frac{e^{\cos(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}_k)/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{\cos(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}_j)/T}} \]

            • \(\mathbf{u}\) is the photo vector and \(\mathbf{v}_k\) the vector of the caption of class \(k\). \(K\) is the number of candidate captions, and \(T = 0.01\) as in the loss.
            • The ranking needs only the cosines. The probabilities add the temperature and depend on the other candidates.

            Common mistakes

            Debug tip. If a zero-shot result looks wrong, test with a short list of two or three captions you are sure about, then add classes. And test several templates: they can change results by several points on a small set.

            In Python

            import numpy as np
names = ["dolphin", "sea turtle", "clownfish"]
cos = np.array([0.276, 0.245, 0.205])       # the hammerhead photo against "a photo of a ...": its true class is not offered
z = cos / 0.01
p = np.exp(z - z.max()); p /= p.sum()
print(np.round(p, 3))
print(names[p.argmax()])
            [0.956 0.043 0.001]
dolphin

            The probabilities add to 1 over the captions offered, so the hammerhead photo is called a dolphin with 96%. The model has no way to say “none of these”.

            The same in murky water

            Guess first. In the chapter on murky water, a ResNet-18 (a network trained on web photos) gave more shark confidence to photos without a shark as the water got murkier. CLIP was trained on 400 million pairs of web photos and captions, probably with many kinds of water. Does it stay right, and would “in murky water” in the captions help?

            On these eight photos, CLIP’s top captions are right less often as the simulated water deepens. The shark mass of a photo is the probability that CLIP gives to the five shark captions among the nine species captions. A false alarm is a high shark mass on a photo that shows no shark. For the three photos without a shark, with the captions “a photo of a ...”, the mean shark mass is below 10% from 0 m to 16 m. After that it grows. This simple depth model of light in water is not a measurement of Mumbai water.

            1. Choose “Dolphin (not a shark)” and drag the depth from 0 to 30 m. The photo darkens, and “Any shark caption” (the shark mass) in the readout rises from 2% to 52%.
            2. In the right chart the solid teal line is the share of the 8 photos with the right species: 88% at 0 m, 75% at 20 m, 50% at 30 m. Choose the template “a photo of a ... in murky water” to compare.

            Probability of the nine captions at this depth

            This photo against depth: CLIP and ResNet-18

            Species right on 8 photos, for three templates

            At 0, 10, 20 and 30 m, CLIP’s mean shark mass over the three photos without a shark is 1%, 3%, 21% and 50%, with the captions “a photo of a ...”.

            How it works

            Take 20 m, with the template “a photo of a ...”. Choose the dolphin, clownfish and sea turtle photos in turn and read “Any shark caption” in the readout.

            Shark mass at 20 m:40%dolphin+23%clownfish+1%sea turtle=64%sum÷ 3 =21%mean over the three photos

            ResNet-18 chooses among 1,000 classes and CLIP among nine captions, so the two models answer different questions. Only the kind of failure is comparable: false alarms that grow with depth. The fold has the ResNet-18 numbers. With eight photos, one photo changing its top caption moves the share with the right species by 12.5 points. Over the 16 depths (0 to 30 m in steps of 2 m), the mean of that share is 66% with “a photo of a ...” and 63% when “in murky water” is added. The two differ by less than one photo, so these photos give no evidence that naming the water helps.

            Common belief. A model trained on a vast and varied set of photos will cope with murky water.

            Why it fails. The figure shows wrong species and growing false alarms on these photos. The mix of water in CLIP’s 400 million photos is unknown, so the cause is not tested.

            Better account. A wide training set widens what a model can do, and a kind of water can still be rare in it, so test with photos from that water.

            Quick quiz

            Why is a false alarm a problem for SharkCam, a robot that flags sharks in dive photos for people to check?

            A false alarm is a dive frame that the robot would flag as a shark, and the people checking the flags would spend time on empty water.

            What would you need to claim that “in murky water” in the captions helps?

            You need more photos, so that a difference is larger than the 12.5 points of one photo.

            Go deeper the figure, caveats, a bridge to my work about 4 min

            Terms

            depth.py
            the simple model of light in water used in C3, now run in your browser

            Reading the figure

            The CLIP numbers are computed in advance (the eight photos at 16 depths), while the photo you see is made in your browser by the same model as in C3. With the template "a photo of a ..." the model names the right species on 7 of 8 photos at 0 m and 10 m. It is right on 6 of 8 at 20 m and 4 of 8 at 30 m. For the five shark photos the mean shark mass is 1.00 at 0 m, 0.89 at 20 m and 0.64 at 30 m. At 30 m two of the four wrong answers are “hammerhead” (the clownfish and the spadenose photo) and two are “dolphin” (the milk shark photos). A hammerhead is a shark that is photographed in blue open water, and a deep blue frame may resemble such photos. This is a reading of the pattern and was not tested.

            The ResNet comparison and the size of the test

            In C3 the ResNet-18 had the 1,000 ImageNet classes and shark confidence counts three of them. Here CLIP chooses among nine captions, five of which are sharks, so the two curves answer slightly different questions, and CLIP is not shown to be better or worse. Only the kind of failure is comparable: false alarms that grow with depth. The ResNet-18 curves are the stored ones of C3, which gives 0.46 for the non-shark photos at 30 m. Eight photos is a small set, and one photo changing its answer moves the accuracy by 12.5 points. The dips and recoveries of the accuracy curve rest on a few photos, so they should not be read as a pattern. An example is the rise to 7 of 8 at 20 m and 22 m for the template with “in murky water”, followed by a drop to 4 of 8 at 24 m.

            For ResNet-18 the shark confidence of the same three photos is 30% at 0 m, because it calls the dolphin photo a shark class. At 10, 20 and 30 m it is 6%, 21% and 46%.

            Does naming the water help?

            The three templates give 49% (bare names), 66% ("a photo of a ...") and 63% ("... in murky water") when averaged over the 16 depths. Adding the water to the caption was better at 20 m (7 of 8 photos right against 6 of 8) and worse at 0 m (5 of 8 against 7 of 8). The averages differ by less than one photo. So on these photos there is no evidence that it helps. The idea behind it is reasonable, since the text side can be changed at no training cost. A fair test needs many more photos and several dives (the group split of A4).

            In my own work

            Bridge to my work. In-Place Test-Time Training, a method from ByteDance Seed (Feng and others), treats the down projection of selected MLP blocks as fast weights. It updates them chunk by chunk as the model reads, with a target built from the input. At MBZUAI, in Prof. Salman Khan's group, I am porting the method from text models to a Qwen vision-language model, so that it can adapt to an input after deployment. My motivation is recognising a shark when the water, light and animals change between dives (C3, project page). The failure on this page is that kind of change. How a vision-language model is built from a ViT and a language model comes in E4.

            Common mistakes

            Debug tip. Run the no-shift check of C3 here as well: at 0 m the figure must show the unchanged photo and the clear-water numbers. A curve that is already poor at 0 m is not caused by murky water: look for a bug, a bad caption list, or a photo that the model gets wrong even in clear water (the spadenose photo is called a milk shark at 0 m).

            Exercises

            Theory

            1. theory A batch has N = 8 pairs and the model gives all 64 cosines the same value. Find the row loss, the column loss and the batch loss. Then find the loss for N = 32,768 and say what it tells you about training with a small batch.

              Hint

              When all entries of a row are equal, softmax gives the entries the same probability, 1/N.

            2. theory The top two cosines of a photo are 0.337 and 0.331. Find the odds between the two captions at T = 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001. Then find the probability of the top caption at the four temperatures if only these two captions are offered.

            3. theory Show that the loss does not change if you add the same constant to all cosines. Then show that dividing all cosines by 2 has the same effect on the loss as doubling T. What does the first fact say about the "gap" of the previous section?

              Hint

              Write the softmax of a row with \(s_{ij}+c\) and take the factor \(e^{c/T}\) out of the numerator and the denominator.

            4. theory A text encoder reads the vector at the end token and a ViT reads the class token. Explain what the two have in common and why the text encoder uses a causal mask, using D4.

            Practice

            1. practice Use the four-photo matrix of the code block. Compute the loss at T = 0.03 and 0.003. Then search a grid of T from 0.001 to 1 for the lowest loss, and say why the best T is not 0.01 for this batch.

            2. practice Build a made-up batch of 6 pairs with cosines on the diagonal near 0.32 and off the diagonal near 0.22 plus noise of size 0.03 (use a seeded generator). Compute the loss at T = 0.01 for 200 batches and report the mean and the share of rows in which the diagonal is not the top entry.

            3. practice Use the cosines of the code block for the hammerhead photo and rank the nine species. Then offer only the three sharks "milk", "Ganges" and "spadenose" (the true class is missing). What are the probabilities, and what does this say about the class list?

            Think deeper

            1. open SharkCam wants to flag the Ganges shark, which has three records in the made-up table and almost no photos. Would you use zero-shot CLIP with a caption for it? What would you measure, with which photos, and what would a safe use look like given the model card says deployed use is out of scope?

            2. open Design an experiment that tests whether CLIP uses the colour of the water as a cue for "hammerhead". Say which edits you would make to the photos, how many photos you would use, and how you would tell a true cue from the noise of a small set.

            3. open The captions of the web are written by people, mostly in English, and describe what they find worth posting. Name two ways this could change what CLIP knows about sharks of the Mumbai coast, and one test for the two.

            Come back later

            Answer after two days and again after a week, without looking back.

            Write the contrastive loss of a batch in words, say what its value is when all cosines are equal, and say what the temperature does.

            Take a softmax over the row of cosines of a photo, divided by T, and take the negative log of the diagonal entry. Do the same down the column of a caption and average the two. With equal cosines the loss is ln N. A small T stretches gaps so that a difference of 0.01 is a clear preference (matrix, temperature).

            In E1 a ViT keeps its call when patches are moved. How is that related to the finding here that CLIP's calls change as the frame gets darker?

            Both say that these encoders lean on colour and texture. In E1 this keeps the call when layout is destroyed. Here it shifts the call when the colours are changed. Neither shows that colour is the only cue (E1, murky, B9).

            A4 says a model that never flags the Ganges shark is 99.5% accurate on the catch table. What is the zero-shot counterpart on this page, and what would you report instead of accuracy?

            A caption list that gives a common shark for all Ganges photos can still look good on accuracy over many species. Report the recall for the rare class with an interval, and the false alarms, as in A4.
